newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: U.K. opposes rigid stability pact - Bank governor.
newsitem.headline: U.K. opposes rigid stability pact - Bank governor.

text.p: Britain opposes any attempt to define an overly rigid stability pact for future members of a European single currency, Bank of England governor Eddie George said.
"We are pragmatic. We think it is not very wise to introduce hard and fast rules," he told journalists.
Some countries, notably Germany, have pressed for clear limits on the freedom of single-currency members to run up budget deficits. They want fines imposed when limits are exceeded.

George, who was on a 24-hour visit to Lisbon, said that all potential members of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) agreed on the principles that lay behind the stability pact -- the need for firm fiscal discipline -- but differed on how the pact should operate.
He said that Britain, which has yet to decide whether it would eventually join a single currency, should be in a position to meet the economic tests for membership.
Britain "had a perfectly respectable chance of meeting the criteria without any fudge," he said.
EMU sets a series of stiff tests in areas such as budget deficit and inflation that candidates must pass in 1997 to be eligible to join the single currency at its planned launch in 1999.
